INTERNATIONAL WHALING COMMISSION
subsubtopic: POSITION TAKEN BY CANADA AT CONFERENCE-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, to propose a motion of urgent and pressing necessity. 1 am afraid my preamble may be a bit long, but it is very important.
Whereas the threat of extinction of many species of whales is well known, since there is no commercial whaling currently carried on by Canada, since Canada has voted against the moratorium on distant water whaling at the recent meetings of the IWC, in spite of the fact that 16 countries, including the United States, Britain, Australia and New Zealand supported a commercial moratorium, whereas Canadian officials have routinely ignored the recommendation of conservationists, and whereas the Department of the Environment has been given no role in formulating this important policy, all of which subjects Canada to growing international criticism, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon):
That this House recognize the serious threat posed by commercial whaling to the survival of all species of whales and record its opposition to the actions of Canada in voting against the moratorium at the IWC meetings held yesterday and today in England and that this House direct the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to make a statement on motions to explain the actions of his officials.

speechtext:

That this government immediately abolish the Metric Commission, thereby saving the Canadian taxpayer over $8 million this fiscal year.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to Standing Order 43. Whereas Canada signed the UN convention on elimination of all forms of discrimination against women last week in Copenhagen at the world conference of the UN decade for women, and whereas it will not be possible for Canada to ratify this convention as long as discriminating features exist in such federal legislation as the Indian Act, the Income Tax Act, the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Canada Pension Plan Act, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell):
That this House instruct the government to introduce as soon as possible such amendments to the Indian Act, the Income Tax Act, the Unemployment Insurance Act, the Canada Pension Plan Act and other relevant acts as are necessary to remove existing discrimination against women, thereby enabling the governmment to ratify the UN convention on elimination of all forms of discrimination against women.

Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, to ask for the unanimous consent of the House to introduce a motion dealing with a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Considering the systematic use made by the Quebec separatists of the phrase "le federal" to refer to the Canadian government, considering the frequent use of this phrase made by parliamentary reporters of the CBC French network and by the media in general, considering the disparaging connotation that such an overuse gave to the word "le federal", I move, seconded by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Lapointe):

subsubtopic: STATUS OF BRANCH LINES PUT INTO PERMANENT NETWORK-MOTION UNDER S O. 43

Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) has caused great anxiety and uncertainty for many western farmers by raising the question of whether he would honour a commitment by the previous minister of transport to guarantee service on some 30 branch lines by placing them in the permanent network. In view of the fact that this uncertainty is causing railway and elevator companies to postpone upgrading and maintenance programs until the government makes up its mind, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor):
That the Minister of Transport end the uncertainty surrounding the future of these branch lines by stating that he will not change the status of any branch lines put into the permanent network by the previous minister.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the President of the Treasury Board. The minister, because of his position while a member of the opposition, will be familiar with the subject matter covered by the first report of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts which was presented to the House last Friday. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, since the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) is present, I will raise my point of order. Last night during the late show I asked the same question of the parliamentary secretary who was representing the minister. When I brought the statement of the minister on April 17 and my concern over the subsequent statements made by the minister that the government was considering export taxes on natural gas to the attention of the parliamentary secretary, he told me that I could rely on the word of the minister. July 22, 1980

said that that was not part of his policy, but today completely reversing himself and swallowing himself. speechtext:
1.	Will over-the-side sales be permitted by the government and, if so (a) under what conditions (b) who will receive the benefits of such arrangements (c) will guarantees by the government be part of any such arrangements?
2.	Will government officials be involved in the negotiations at public expense and, if so, will the Crown be compensated for its involvement in the negotiations and, if so, by whom?

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: OVER-THE-S1DE SALES
speechtext:
1. Yes.
(a) East coast
"Over-the-side" sales will be permitted in 1980 where potential catches are surplus to the processing and marketing capability of Canadian industry or where no domestic market exists at acceptable economic return to fishermen. The program was initiated at the request of the fishermen, through their representative organizations. We do not permit as part of our general policy "over-the-side" sales arrangements to prejudice the existing markets of the Canadian industry. Preferential treatment is given to countries with which Canada has marketing or other special interests and foreign partners will normally be restricted to countries which do not use the purchases in direct marketing competition with Canadian products. Foreign vessels involved should be from countries which have a bilateral fisheries agreement with Canada. Sales "over-the-side" on the Atlantic coast in 1979 represented approximately one percent of the total landings, and less than 0.7 per cent of total value.
West coast
"Over-the-side" sales will be permitted in 1980 for Pacific hake as this species cannot be delivered to Canadian fishing plants without freezing-at-sea and as only one Canadian freezer trawler is available on the west coast, other Canadian fishermen must have the opportunity to deliver fish using "over-the-side" sales of fish to foreign vessels.
(b)	The benefits will be with the fishermen because they have a market for fish at an acceptable economic return which might not otherwise be the case. The British Columbia fishing industry is also directly involved and benefit from "over-the-side" sales on the west coast.
(c)	As an extension of the department's commensurate benefits policy, a direct allocation of fish which have not been traditionally fished offshore by Canadians, may be granted in return for firm commitments to provide freezer trawlers for a number of months and purchase fish at predetermined prices.
2. Yes-east coast. No-west coast. The Crown on the east coast will be largely compensated as the harvesting of the direct allocation, as per 1(c), will generate revenues, as an example, in the maritimes arrangement of approximately $125,000 as the foreign vessels will be required to pay all foreign access and fishing fees in accordance with Canadian regulations.

subtopic: MOTION RESPECTING SUMMER RECESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the last few weeks and days many matters of tremendous importance have come before the House. One of the matters which has concerned me is the administration of the law by the ministers upon whom it is imposed. Specifically, 1 should like to deal with the whole area of discretion exercised by a minister, properly or improperly.
Every minister of the Crown has reposed in him by statute, certain discretions and to varying extents. For example, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey) has the ability to choose the method of prosecution in income tax cases. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) has the discretion to determine whether to bring a matter before the Supreme Court of Canada even after all judicial remedies have been exhausted. But nowhere is the discretion wider than that reposed in the minister of immigration.
The Immigration Act sets forth standards to guide in the admission of people into this country. Those standards are rigid, and they need to be, but they are general. There are a certain number of cases in which it is important, however, that we relax those standards. That is the purpose of the discretion. That is the purpose whereby a minister is able to give a ministerial permit. Accordingly, a wide power of discretion is vested with the minister of immigration so that he can relieve or give relief to worthy people who want to come into this country and who are not technically eligible under the act or the regulations.
There is no member in this House who has not pleaded on behalf of a constituent or some other person for the right of that person to be admitted to Canada even though in the circumstances he is technically disqualified. 1 say to this House that every minister, especially the minister of immigration, has to have a sense of compassion and a sense of humanity to deal with cases which, on their facts, cry out for admission. However, there are certain cases in which a minister abuses that right and abuses that discretion.
There has never been any necessary correlation between, on the one hand, a high degree of intelligence, and on the other, good judgment. How many people in this House have we seen with a high degree of intelligence but no judgment, or a lack of judgment?
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) in this session has consistently set a pattern which has demonstrated, certainly to me, a lack of capacity to exercise good judgment. When a prime minister looks for a minister, what does he look for? He looks for integrity. He looks for intelligence, and above all he looks for good judgment. As I say, we have some compelling examples which 1 shall bring before this House which I say to hon. members have rendered ineffective the minister of immigration's functions because of a serious lack of judgment in a number of instances.
It is far too easy to generalize because we all resort to our own sense of prejudices. We have to be specific and draw conclusions from specific instances. No instance is more compelling than the matter which I have drawn to the attention of the House on a couple of occasions, namely, the Calamusa matter. 1 wish to speak to the facts of this case. I know only certain facts but there are many others which are the duty of the minister of immigration to bring before this House in order
July 22, 1980

that we can have a proper accounting with respect to immigration policy.
Mr. Calamusa is 38 years of age. He has six children, three of whom were born in Italy. He came to this country in 1968. However, before he came to Canada he had a serious and long record of criminal activity in Italy. So that the record is clear with respect to this matter, the RCMP report which is reposed in the Federal Court of Canada shows that in 1961 Mr. Calamusa was convicted of aggravated theft in Cagliara, Italy. For this offence he was sentenced to a term of one year in prison and fined 12,000 lira. He said in his testimony that he only served a period of three months.
In 1962 in another part of Italy he was convicted of receiving stolen goods. He was sentenced to 15 days in jail, and fined 4,000 lira.
He was accused and acquitted of swindling in October, 1963. In 1965 he was again convicted of aggravated theft and jailed for a period of eight months and fined 10,000 lira, with a notation on the record "penalty remitted".
Mr. Calamusa came into this country illegally in 1968. He was expelled from Canada in 1970 because he was not eligible to be here. He came illegally, and as a result of his criminal record he was deported. However, he was not only deported on one occasion, he has now been deported on five different occasions.
In court terms, if a person disobeys an order of the court, we call that contempt of court. Mr. Calamusa has consistently shown an absolute disregard for the administrative orders that we know as deportation orders.
The last time that Mr. Calamusa was deported after a jail term, which 1 will refer to later, as a result of a violation of the Immigration Act, he came back here within days, using another name. He has consistently shown contempt for the administration of immigration law.
Far more significant than that is that Calamusa was convicted in 1977 of counterfeiting. He was arrested for counterfeiting in 1975. A bench warrant was issued for his arrest in 1976 by reason of his non-attendance in court; again a form of contempt of court. In 1977 he was picked up by the Metropolitan Toronto police. He was taken into custody, and he was represented by able counsel. At that time he pleaded guilty to possession of counterfeit money. He was sentenced also on an immigration matter and deported to Italy, but he returned to Canada within days.
There is no such offence known to law as just possession of counterfeit money. There is an offence of knowing that you are in possession of counterfeit money. For members in this House who have served in the criminal courts as prosecutors or as defence counsel, one knows that that is a very unique offence. We are not talking about a person who has committed a criminal offence while in Canada in circumstances where, for example, he might have smoked marijuana or where he might have shoplifted or where he might have committed any number of offences, such as impaired driving; we are talking
Summer Recess
about a person who knowingly had in his possession counterfeit money.
I ask the question where did Mr. Calamusa get the counterfeit money? Does the minister know? Has the minister examined the record completely in this case? We are talking about something in terms of the nature of the offence which is unique. But not only that, we have circumstances where Mr. Calamusa has completely exhausted the legal procedure. After he was apprehended the last time, he was again released on bail. A special inquiry was undertaken. It was one of the most exhaustive inquiries which the Hamilton regional people in the department of immigration had conducted. It lasted about 75 hours. The volumes of transcript are literally as long as your arm. The special inquiry officer decided on all of the evidence that Calamusa, who was again ably represented by distinguished counsel, should be deported.
What did Calamusa do after that? He resorted, as was his right, to the Federal Court of Canada, who turned down his appeal. What did he do after that, I ask? He appealed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration to exercise his discretion. At that time the Conservative government was in power and the minister of immigration was Mr. Atkey. I say thank God that in these horrible and rancid set of circumstances the minister decided that this was not a man worthy to be in this country.
Canada is a magnificent country. It has a relatively small population. Last year we took in just over 100,000 people. There was an exodus of approximately 85 so in my opinion we do not have an immigration problem. Canada is a country that holds out its hands. We are a country of immigrants, all of us. This is a great country and that is why we have so many applications to come to this country, but our immigration policy has to be realistic.
As 1 have said before, Mr. Speaker, there is no member of the House who would rather see a minister err on the side of compassion or humanity than myself. However, these circumstances are so outrageous that they bring the whole system of discretion into a state of disrepute.
There are many other questions I wish to raise with respect to this matter. After the expulsion order came about, we know that Calamusa was residing in Niagara Falls. There are certain compassionate grounds which the minister said he acted upon. One was the fact that Calamusa had three children who were born in Canada. We know that the special inquiry into Mrs. Calamusa indicated that she left Canada in 1972 and, when she returned with her husband, she herself was the subject of a deportation. I submit that played very little part in the decision.
The other matter which the minister brought to the attention of the press and the House when asked to account for his action was that he stated that one of Calamusa's sons had serious health problems. I checked that out. 1 went to the the major cities of Italy, whether it be Genoa, Venice or Rome, colitis could be treated as effectively there as in the Sick

July 22, 1980
Summer Recess
Children's Hospital. We know now that in Winnipeg the young Calamusa does not resort to the hospital there, or at least on the evidence he wanted to be close to Sick Children's Hospital for medical attention.
Many other factors rear their heads with respect to this matter. One which interests me is the fact that Mr. Calamusa drove, apparently without appointment, to see the Minister of Employment and Immigration one Saturday morning in June. He drove with his possessions and his family to Winnipeg. There was no phone call. He did not decide to come to Ottawa, but to attend in Winnipeg. He put forward a story which I am sure in his mind was a real plight. In these circumstances the minister answered in this House that he had a certain sense of feeling for the man, and he asked a respected man in the Italian community, Mr. Bova, what he should do in this regard. He also undertook, he said, an investigation with respect to this matter. I hope that discretion was exercised. The following procedure was adopted by the minister, or at least his department.
This family was conveyed by government automobile, limousine-type service, 100 kilometres away to Emerson. What notice was given immigration officials in the United States, as he was being deported from one sovereign country to another? What notice was given to United States officials as to whether they would accept him as a deportee? He was taken across the border for a period no more than five minutes where he was processed. He was then deported, and he and his family were given a ministerial permit to come back into Canada. This limousine service continued, and they were brought back to Winnipeg.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) asked certain germane questions of the minister as to whether this is the standard procedure accorded to every person deported to another country. It offends my sense of intelligence to believe that this is standard procedure. Do you take a person across the border, bring him back and drive him and his family back to where they came from? What representations were made in the meantime that were so compelling?
The minister said that the mayor, or at least the council of Niagara Falls, made certain representations on behalf of this man. I would like to know the nature of those representations. There are certain other people who also made representations, and we will speak more about that later. The point is this. In exercising his discretion the minister established a certain set of criteria. The immigration minister has a certain set of criteria.
The minister exercised his direction even with the flagrant contempt that Calamusa has shown towards the minister's department by returning to Canada, even though Calamusa had committed a serious criminal offence while in Canada illegally. As I mentioned in the House the other day, and the minister did not contradict me, Calamusa is subject to investigation, as are other witnesses. The RCMP are in charge of that investigation which is currently being conducted.
How are we to go back to our constituencies where there are so many worthy cases of people with unblemished records, and
tell them that they cannot come into this country? How do we do that?
Let me give by way of contrast a specific case which has occurred during this session. A man by the name of Gunther Seidel, who is now back in Germany, was a constituent of mine. Mr. Seidel did not have an enviable record when in Germany. He had been convicted of assault in 1976 and received a second sentence for carelessly inflicting bodily harm, and was sentenced to ten days in jail. In 1973 he was convicted of theft. He came to Canada with that criminal record. Mr. Seidel was issued permits to work. One time he forgot, he was a day late, and the permit had expired. As a result we had to resort to a ministerial permit.
During the period of time that Mr. Seidel was in Canada, he married a Canadian citizen and they had a child. He was always gainfully employed as a pastry chef. There was no problem there. The only thing was that he was indebted, like many of us here and many other people, to the tune of $18,000. He had never committed a criminal offence while in Canada and had not done anything to disqualify himself. He had married a Canadian citizen and was father of a child born in Canada. When the minister reviewed this matter, he certainly did not show him the compassion that he exhibited in the case of Calamusa.
When we go back to our ridings on Saturday mornings, we see that the bulk of the cases deal with immigration. I cannot speak for all members, but I can probably speak for the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery) who has consistently taken a deep interest in the whole notion of immigration. Every member of this House is aware of many tear-jerking instances where people ask us to intercede on their behalf. We go to the minister to plead our case. We plead them personally, by mail, and by walking across the floor during question period. We care; everybody cares. However, if this is the way in which discretion is going to be exercised in future, I am going to send all my constituents to the Winnipeg office of Lloyd Axworthy.
I do not want to be misconstrued in terms of the necessity of exercising proper discretion; it is something that must be reposed. My very serious criticism is this: what type of minister, with such a flagrant set of circumstances, would decide in favour of a person who, in my submission, is not worthy of the compassion which the minister says that he extended? The minister's own department said that for very cogent reasons they would not recommend a ministerial permit. What questions do we ask when we hear about this limousine-type of service to Emerson, over the United States border and back? This is a horrible case in terms of the exercise of discretion.
There have been other cases, for example, the Leary case which though not as serious, is an indication of the same type of faulty judgment on the part of the minister of immigration. So I say, Mr. Speaker, that unfortunately, in terms of his track record since February, the minister of immigration, in the very important area of exercising discretion, has fallen upon bad times, if he ever had good discretion in the first place. There is
July 22, 1980

a nexus between good judgment and discretion. To exercise discretion properly demands good judgment.
Many matters have been raised in the last few weeks pertaining to subjects of great importance. The pipeline has certainly been one of the most pre-eminent topics as it well might be. But I say to this House that we have to keep a keen eye on the type of discretion which is being exercised, not only by the minister of immigration but by those responsible for other departments because the people who have the power to administer our laws are as important as the laws themselves. This is a case where I believe the Minister of Employment and Immigration has done a disservice to the House, a disservice to the Canadian people, and certainly a disservice to himself by such a flagrant misuse of his discretion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today's debate on the adjournment motion reminds me of the remarks made by the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnaty-shyn) who, at the outset, was wondering what he was doing in the House on July 21. I suggest several of our colleagues are also wondering what they are doing here. As a matter of fact, ever since our return on Monday, I have had the opportunity to tour various buildings on the Hill, to meet messengers and others servants of the House, and I have come to realize, from what 1 have seen, that the annual leave of a great many people has been delayed by the stubbornness of the New Democratic party-need I mention it-to extend this session which has proved most productive in terms of the adopted legislation. I am somewhat puzzled by the attitude of that party which always claims to favour employment and the work force. How can it justify its stand when on the one hand it is supposed to favour workers while at the same time depriving them of a well-deserved vacation?
During this session, Mr. Speaker, we have been dealing with indeed quite a number of bills, and I should like to mention some of them which are considered most significant. Of course all bills are important, but among those passed by the House, I suggest that the bill introduced by the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) to increase the income supplement for senior citizens is probably the most important, for it has made it possible for them to get assistance on top of their pension.
Unfortunately, however, some provinces, at least one I know about-I do not know what is going on in other Canadian provinces but I know that once again in the province of Quebec, senior citizens will only receive a SI5 increase and that the Quebec government will keep part of it, even though the Minister of National Health and Welfare sent a letter to Mr. Lazure explaining that this increase was intended for people in greater need and that the Government of Canada considered that senior citizens needed this $35 increase in the GIS. According to my information, Mr. Speaker, up to now, the situation is still the same, that is they do not actually
Summer Recess
receive the full amount. This is quite unfortunate for the senior citizens, because the Canadian government had decided that this amount was intended for the people in greater need and it is not being fully paid to them.

subtopic: MOTION RESPECTING SUMMER RECESS
speechtext: This is PQ piracy!

subtopic: MOTION RESPECTING SUMMER RECESS
speechtext:
My colleague here says that it is PQ piracy, Mr. Speaker. That is right on. Each time the Canadian government makes payments to senior citizens, the Quebec government, in this case at least, lays hands on them and deprives the people of part of the money.
During this session, Mr. Speaker, we passed a bill concerning an employment tax credit which was voted by the House, and I was quite surprised to see that only one party was against this bill, namely the NDP. I think that NDP members voted once again against their own interests, because how can they be unaware of the situation? If workers are hired by various employers who benefit from the employment tax credit across Canada, these workers might be members of the CLC, and the wages earned by these workers might accrue to the CLC and indirectly to the NDP, since that party actually gets a very important contribution from the CLC. Therefore they really voted against their interests.
I have seen members of the Progressive Conservative Party during the debate on that legislation make representations, ask for explanations in Committee of the Whole to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) and later on, when the question was put after they heard explanations from the minister, they voted with the government in support of employment tax credit program. The only party that voted against was the NPD, and I thought they were voting against themselves.
As far as other bills were concerned, Mr. Speaker, this past year, there has been, of course, the veterans' bill that was sponsored by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald). It included substantial amendments granting our veterans very important rights that were lacking under the previous act.
And as stated by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard), we have seen in this House since April 14, since the opening of this new parliament, 25 pieces of legislation that were introduced and passed, and I feel that this House can boast to all Canadians that we have been very productive. These were significant measures for the well-being of all Canadians, including, of course, the province of Quebec, all Quebeckers. Clearly then, after that period from April 14 until Friday last, that very productive period, hon. members from the Progressive Conservative Party also were in agreement that we should adjourn.
I listened yesterday to the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn), who asked what we were doing here. He was referring to the fact that he wanted a few days' holidays,

July 22, 1980
Summer Recess
as a number of other members to go and explain the measures that were enacted in this House to Quebeckers, to Canadians, to people in Saskatchewan, what the purport and the thrust of these measures were, and tell the people in our constituencies what benefits they can expect from these bills. Indeed, several programs were designed for the benefit of the workers. That could be explained. The only party, of course, that would not allow, as I suggested at the outset, the security staff, the pages or the messengers to take a well-deserved holiday, the only party bent on preventing that from occurring is the New Democratic Party who say they require certain guarantees and by the same token question the Congress, decision and President Carter's word.
Mr. Speaker, what conclusion can be drawn from such a situation? Is this normal, given the circumstances, when you look at the situation in which the messengers and other support staff of the House find themselves? I am told there are about 3,000 people working here as members of the House support staff and that probably 1,000 would be deprived of their well-deserved vacation as a result of this systematic blocking or whatever you may call this filibuster by the NDP members.
Is it in fact possible then-and we are praised for that and considered even as being on the workers' side but they are preventing workers from going on vacation. Where is the logic in all that? And they seem happy about it. Mr. Speaker, since April 14, we also had to pass a bill a few days before Canada Day-July 1-on the national anthem "O Canada". I believe it was one of the great moments of the House to see "O Canada" officially adopted as the national anthem of this country, and I remember quite well that on that day, in this House, we sang our national anthem to show that the passing of that bill was really desired by all parties in the House.
Then, Mr. Speaker, in the last days of the session, on July 17 to be more specific, the gas pipeline issue came up followed by the NDP request for guarantees. When we see that the New Democratic Party which is in office in Saskatchewan is against the position taken by the same party here in the House of Commons, we wonder where the logic is in the position taken by the NDP members in the House and we ask what their policy really is. When we refer to the official report in last week's Hansard more specifically that for July 17, and when we think of the economic fall-outs in Canada, the revenues could be used to create new jobs and increase productivity, we find that the hon. Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) stated, as reported on page 3043:
According to estimates-
-the pre-build section!
-will result in direct capital expenditures in Canada of a total of $1.6 billion, the benefits of which would be fell right across the country in terms of jobs and output.
How can a party which claims to be fighting for the workers of this country be against such a project? That is the question all parties in the House except, of course, the New Democratic Party, are asking, for these members are working against themselves and against the workers they say they are proud to represent. I think perhaps they will have to consult Mr. McDermott, the president of the Canadian Labour Congress, to know whether indeed he agrees with them when such investments are made on a national scale. Those people could perhaps help them in the next election campaign so that they can have more money at their disposal. Now they are again voting against them, and thus preventing their financial support from doing its job.
Of course it can be argued also that direct and indirect manpower needs generated by the pre-build and related works could mean 150,000 man-years between 1980 and 1984. What kind of a country can refuse such an investment, such an employment opportunity? I think, Mr. Speaker, it is not possible at this time to refuse that when knowing what guarantees are provided. We read in Hansard, page 3053, what the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said in this House when answering a question, and I quote:
I have heard one of my friends in the NDP saying that one Congress does not bind another Congress. He knows, or he should know, that there are only two parties in the United States, and after the election there will be either a Republican majority or a Democrat majority in the Congress. What is interesting in this case is that we have the unanimous consent of both parties in the U.S. Congress and a commitment to see to it that this line is completed by the end of 1985.
Mr. Speaker, as matters now stand it does not make any difference what happens in the United States after November, whether the Republicans or the Democrats are elected, they have unanimously accepted in Congress that the line should be completed before the end of 1985.
Subsequently, Mr. Speaker, the President of the United States wrote to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) assuring him that such was the situation. Is the New Democratic Party going to challenge the word of the President of the United States? Many newspapers editorializing on this issue conclude that we have in the House of Commons a party that is challenging the unanimous consent of the Democrats and Republicans in Congress and also the word of the President of the United States.
What sort of logic inhabits those people? I think they are trying to drum up some publicity, but it is turning against them, Mr. Speaker, because much of their credibility is being lost over the situation. Naturally, the west is involved. But what will happen to Quebec and Ontario? Many people have expressed concern over the situation. If we take Hansard for July 17, on page 3062 we find the following in reply to a question put by the hon. member for Chateauguay (Mr. Watson). The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) replied, and I quote:
July 22, 1980

I have already indicated that Quebec and Ontario will share among themselves, simply from that first part of the project, $360 million. In addition, when the entire project is put in motion, Quebec and Ontario will benefit from an additional amount of $1.57 billion, for a total for those two provinces of $1.93 billion.
Mr. Speaker, such are the benefits which the provinces, some eastern provinces like Ontario and Quebec, will derive, an industry in Contrecoeur, which is not far from Sorel, I think it is in the riding of Vercheres or Richelieu, was even mentioned. Summer Recess

subtopic: MOTION RESPECTING SUMMER RECESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I plan during the next few minutes to discuss some items-three, four, or five depending on the time-of concern to the people of Bow River and t believe also to the people of Canada. The first one is conservation of gas and oil. We hear much discussion about gas and oil, but there has been very little discussion about the conservation of gas and oil.
The other day I had the opportunity of asking the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) a question about the wastage of gas from pipelines. Some say we have in Canada half a million miles of gas and oil pipelines. Certainly we have well over 200,000 or 300,000 miles of them, and the law requires that they be traversed in some manner at least once every three years. Many companies are traversing these by helicopter or airplane, and unless oil or gas has leaked to the point where it has spread over quite a large area, it is not discernible. The lines are not walked except in a very few cases. Consequently it is very difficult, if not impossible, to estimate the large volumes of gas and oil lost in this country through complete waste, and yet we ask our people to cut down on their mileage and to conserve gas and oil in every way possible, and properly so.
1 suggest that the government and the corporations of this country set an example for the people by conserving these very valuable resources to the greatest possible extent. The other day 1 suggested one means which has come into vogue with regard to finding gas leaks, and that is through the use of dogs. Many people thought it was some sort of joke, but a large gas company in Texas telephoned my office about three or four days later wanting to get particulars of this method of detecting gas leaks. The Lone Star Gas Company has more than 3,300 miles of gas lines in Texas and the U.S.A. It is now in touch with the Avery Kennels to see what can be done in this regard. Wastage is no joke to the Lone Star Gas Company in Texas, and I do not think wastage from the lines in this country should be a joke either.
It has already been proved that dogs are able to find leaks with very little training. As a matter of fact, in 1978 dogs found ten leaks in a 30-mile line in the Redwater area of Alberta which had earlier been checked by helicopter. No leaks were found by helicopter, and then the line was checked by electronic flame packs. No leaks were found, yet the dogs found ten. How many thousands of cubic feet of gas are wasted through not detecting these leaks and not detecting them at an early stage?
Dogs have been able to do tremendous things. A brother of the dogs at the Avery Kennels is now doing narcotics work with the U.S. government. It is spotting narcotics and doing a splendid job, I am told. In Texas two similar dogs are involved with dope detection and doing a splendid job. If we can use our dogs to help conserve a few thousand cubic feet of gas, that would be a very valuable service to this country. We can talk about conservation all we like, but if we ignore some of the wastage which is apparent, then we lose all credibility with the
July 22, 1980
rank and file of the people who are asked to deny themselves in order to conserve gas.
I hope the Prime Minister and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) are prepared to provide a grant which would allow the continued training and managing of dogs so that we can find out what their capabilities are to more distinct degree. Already there are a number of companies which are interested in this particular phase, but they want to make comparisons with dog detection, electronic flame and helicopter methods of detecting gas. The government has a responsibility to take the lead in providing the means for finding these gas leaks. Trans-Canada PipeLines Limited, Saskatchewan Power Corporation, Alberta Gas TrunkLines, Alberta Government Telephones, B.C. Hydro, West Coast Transmission, Norcin Resources plus some other 19 companies in the United States are interested in using dogs to detect leaks. There is a major need for a comparison study and for charts to guide these companies in the detection of gas leaks. It would require a grant of $70,000 to buy the modern equipment and to acquire the knowledge to work it with trained dogs and handlers.

We could also develop the method using flame ionization equipment as well as with dogs. This system has tremendous possibilities. I ask the government to give some very careful thought to the conserving of gas in this way. I am referring to gas which has already been produced and paid for. It is criminal to see it simply being wasted.
The next point of conservation which I have in mind deals with the carburetors in our cars. There was some brief discussion on this matter. My executive assistant, Joe Williams, and I have carried out some research. We find that in Canada the average mileage for a carburetor is 47.1 miles per gallon. In the U.S.A. the average mileage is 42 miles per gallon, and in Japan it is 62.4 miles per gallon. We all know that the weight of the vehicle, the carburetor and the pollution controls are the factors which determine the mileage, of a carburetor.
There are a number of anomalies which exist in this area. I have seen a much larger car give better mileage than a smaller car with the same pollution controls. It would indicate that in many cases, but not all cases, the carburetor is the answer.
Every once in a while we hear of people who claim to have knowledge of automobile companies buying carburetors from inventors. There are inventors who have claimed that they have invented carburetors which could get 50 miles or 60 miles per gallon. Some years ago while working for the highways department in Alberta, I received a letter from an individual in Montana telling me that he had a carburetor which would get 50 miles to the gallon. I was interested immediately and I wrote back to him. Approximately two weeks later I received an answer, and he informed me that he had sold the invention to one of the large automobile companies in the United States.
If these automobile companies are buying inventions, such as carburetors, which are designed to give better mileage, and not putting them in their cars, then it is criminal conspiracy
July 22, 1980

against the people of our country. There are also people in Canada who have claimed that they have invented carburetors, sold them, and then heard no more. There is some indication that the large automobile companies want to keep these carburetors and eventually bring them on the market some years down the road. That is not good enough. We are facing shortages. We are today trying to conserve natural gas even though we have a surplus. We are trying to conserve gasoline because we do not have a surplus.
When an automobile company has at its disposal, if indeed they have, carburetors which would double the mileage per gallon of their automobiles and which they are not using, then in my view that is criminal conspiracy. The government should carry out a very careful investigation into this whole matter, and determine whether or not these auto giants are holding these carburetors. If they are, then they should be prosecuted to the limit because they are certainly not acting as good corporate citizens should in the interests of the country.
The department is now doing something along these lines. They are now providing for an average and hoping to get 26.4 miles and 28.8 miles per gallon respectively by 1981 and 1982 in all passenger cars. We must also ask ourselves why it is that Japanese cars can get 62.4 miles to the gallon. Weight is one of the factors, but the carburetors, 1 think, provide a more complete answer.
The whole matter of conservation of gas and fuel, by whatever means, should be led by the government to encourage our people to conserve. I went into the home of a senior citizen a couple of years ago. It was at the time that the government was asking people to conserve energy. It was a chilly night and the house was cold. The father had a heavy wool sweater on, and his wife was wearing a similar garment, but they were chilly. I asked why their house was so cold. As a matter of fact, I kept my overcoat on. The fellow said, "Well, the government wants us to conserve energy, and we think that we should do our part". They were excellent citizens, trying to co-operate with the government by conserving energy.
When we hear of corporate citizens doing the reverse, it only discredits them in the minds of the people. Conservation is an important item and I do not think that it can be over-emphasized. But let us not put all the emphasis on asking our people to conserve energy before we are willing to do everything within our power to make sure we detect the wastage, whether it be in gas lines, oil lines, carburetors, or the use of the fuel itself.
The second item which 1 would like to discuss is somewhat agricultural in scope. While we were in government our minister of transport, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazan-kowski), did a tremendous job during the few months he was there. As a matter of fact whenever 1 talk to farmers throughout western Canada, the name of Mazankowski is symbolic with action, sincerity, and help for the people of the land. Some of the things which the hon. member for Vegreville had done while in that position are still paying dividends. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), to his credit, is following along the lines in many areas which were initiated by Mr. Summer Recess
Mazankowski. He is on the same track in many things, but he has slowed down the train.
The people of western Canada want action with regard to the sale of their grain. They are not getting that action as fast as they would like. More hopper cars are coming, and the hon. member for Vegreville appointed probably the top man in Canada with regard to knowledge of the whole transportation system as it affects farming. Dr. Hugh Horner, to do a study on grain transportation.
I had the pleasure of watching Dr. Horner work in the legislature for many years, and I was always amazed at how he kept himself informed on all aspects. He knows agriculture like a book, and he knows the transportation system. If he is given a free hand he will do wonders for the transportation of our grain. The hon. member for Vegreville predicted a 20 per cent increase in sales. Statistics show that there has already been a 17.6 increase this year and that it will likely go to over 20 per cent if things continue to work well.
I think we should pay tribute to people like the hon. member for Vegreville who worked long hours and dedicated themselves to making sure they did something for the people who really needed help.

subtopic: MOTION RESPECTING SUMMER RECESS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION RESPECTING SUMMER RECESS
speechtext:
Our farmers need help. Many of them are living below the poverty line. They are not being paid as much as they should be for their grain. I hope the day will soon come when they receive a cost plus price for the crops they raise. Food is an important item, Mr. Speaker, and we cannot expect them to sell for less than it costs to produce, year in and year out. They should have a cost plus margin of profit in order that they may enjoy the good things of this country. We are making progress, and I hope we can do even better in the months ahead.
Branch lines are another matter of vital concern which the hon. member examined in a realistic way. He said, "Where there are elevators or where there is some sense in keeping a line, then we will keep those lines." He made no bones about it, and the farmers are thankful. If the present Minister of Transport were to accept the program outlined by the hon. member for Vegreville he would be on the right track, but if he starts talking about this line, that line, and the other line for some reason being not relevant to moving grain or coal or whatever has to be moved, he will be doing this country a disservice. Where there are elevators on branch lines that the companies are prepared to keep, elevators to which the farmers have been hauling grain for years, those lines should be kept. They are part of our transportation system and are necessary for getting the grain to market. Every extra mile a farmer has to haul his grain adds to the cost of production and the farmer must, of course, increase the cost of his product if he is to make a reasonable living.
I know of one branch line that was declared valid until the year 2000 under the jurisdiction of the hon. member for

July 22, 1980
Summer Recess
Vegreville, but it is now in jeopardy because his recommendation is apparently not being followed. There are active elevators on the line and the farmers want to haul their grain to them. The elevators are surrounded by coulees and it would be difficult for the farmers to go elsewhere, so I would urge the Minister of Transport to look again at that particular branch line abandonment. He would do himself credit if he were to follow the program initiated by his predecessor. If the Liberal party is looking for credibility in the west, this is one way they could get it-by doing what is right, and it is right to keep these lines operative.
Another matter that concerns me is the problem of level crossings, Mr. Speaker. I learned that at a western hearing the Canadian Transport Commission gave the CNR permission to remove a crossing that has been in service for many years. The village council, the elevator companies and the people in the area cannot understand why. The crossing has been there for 30 or 40 or even 50 years, and is still being used. Indeed, it is still required, but the CNR has been given permission to remove it. I have written to the commission asking for the rationale for moving the crossing, as in my view the decision does not make sense. This is the type of thing that brings discredit on the government, when it permits its appointed board to take such actions. Railway crossings should not be removed simply because the company wants them removed. If a crossing is being used it should be kept.
The next item I should like to deal with briefly is the matter of waste. People bring this to my attention at almost every meeting I hold in my constituency. I should like to deal with three or four items-and I do so respectfully, in the hope that it will have some effect on the program followed by the government.
The first item concerns a fishing vessel. This matter was brought to light by the Auditor General, but it is still in limbo. It is a fiasco that the government should take steps to set right. Apparently Cl DA decided to carry out additional work on a vessel which it had contracted to build for Argentina in 1973 at a cost of $308,000. But it cost an additional $357,000, making a total cost of $665,000. It was then delivered to Argentina but Argentina would not accept it because it was in terrible condition. In 1976 the government spent another $745,000 on it, bringing the cost up to $1,410,000. It was again presented to Argentina and again Argentina would not accept it as it was not satisfactory. Argentina would not even accept it as a gift, Mr. Speaker. In 1976 Cl DA applied to the government and got ministerial approval to spend $3.5 million on another fishing vessel. That second vessel was not acquired but CIDA took $720,000 of the funds allotted for it and spent that money on the first vessel. Now the price of the first vessel was $2.1 million.

subtopic: MOTION RESPECTING SUMMER RECESS
speechtext: Is this a true story?

subtopic: MOTION RESPECTING SUMMER RECESS
speechtext:
This is a true story, Mr. Speaker. Ripley should have been told about it. In 1978 Argentina again refused to accept the vessel-after Canadians had spent $2.1 million on it! It rests in limbo and now the government is apparently
considering spending more than $2.1 million so that the vessel can be presented as a gift to a country that apparently needs it. If this is an example of CIDA's activities, then it should be abandoned. It should be held accountable and responsible.
Just today the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) asked the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) what was being done to make sure that the extravagance and waste evident in our buildings are curtailed. The minister answered that they were taking steps to appoint a project manager and to do certain other things to keep control and make government accountable. That is fine, but unless we start dealing with some of these items that are bringing discredit on Canada, something is wrong. The government should find out who is responsible. Do they know what they are doing or is some landlubber in charge of building these vessels? The matter should be investigated and whoever is responsible should be severely disciplined.
That is one example of waste that I am sure no member of the government is proud of, and as a Canadian I am not proud of it. We should correct it and make sure that it does not happen again.
Another example is the Calgary airport. I dealt with this subject briefly in question period today. The Calgary airport was started in 1967. As a matter of fact I was employed by the department of highways at the time and negotiated the price for the right-of-way with the Canadian government for the Calgary airport. The land was acquired by 1969 and the federal cheque came to the Alberta government approximately in 1970 or early in 1971. The actual planning started in 1967. The actual construction started in 1974. In spite of that seven-year time span to plan and prepare the plans and get concurrence by everyone involved, construction started only in 1974 and the airport was completed in 1977 and officially opened.
But here is the sad story. We have an excellent airport in Calgary. I am not complaining about the airport. In fact I commend the government for building the airport and having vision for the future in so far as the vision has gone with respect to that airport. What I am complaining about is the lack of planning to the point where alterations and changes are made after a building is under construction. A layman, whether he has ever had a hammer in his hand or not, knows that if plans are changed after tenders are let it will cost additional money. There will be penalties involved, things to change and additional materials to be bought.
What happened with the Calgary airport? In 1974 the plans were ready and the cost was estimated at $21.3 million. The square footage was 452,530. By the time that airport was completed in 1977, the cost had risen from $21.3 million to $75.7 million, an increase of $54.4 million, which is more than twice the original estimated cost. It is an increase of 255 per cent. The square footage had increased from 452,530 to 720,550, or an increase of another 268,020 square feet.
July 22, 1980

These are typical examples of what 1 am trying to point out.
1 know this situation happened in the past and under a Liberal administration, but that is not the point I want to make. My point is that people's money is being wasted. If we had wanted an airport consisting of 720,000 square feet, why was it not planned that way? Why did we not go to the various airline companies before letting tenders. Why did we not get a final plan, let it out to tender, and then stick to it after consulting with all parties involved?
I raise this point for two reasons. First, every year the government is building new buildings, new airports, etc. 1 say let us make sure that we do not change plans once we get the contract under way. Let us make sure we do all that work before, and present a final plan to the Treasury Board and then have the money allotted based on that amount.
When I served on the public accounts committee last year 1 was amazed to hear civil servants, when they were trying to explain this type of thing, say that to alleviate the problem we will have project managers. Project managers have not suddenly been manufactured or invented. In Alberta we had project managers oversee the building of highways in 1950 and in 1960. It was nothing new. The provinces used project managers to oversee construction of public buildings. So 1 ask why has it taken so long for the federal department to have someone on the job responsible for the construction of buildings? Although 1 am not a member of the public accounts committee this year, when I was a member last year 1 asked what happened to the man in charge and there was no answer from the civil servants. Someone suggested he was promoted and got an increase in pay. I do not know whether he did or not, but he should have been fired, and he should have been held responsible and accountable. 1 do not think it is right to simply pass these costs on to the people and just let it go at that. It is the people's money and we, as members of Parliament, are responsible for that.
I have another example of high level spending. When the hon. member for Leeds-Grenville (Mr. Cossitt) raised the point a few weeks ago in this House about a representative of Canada getting lavish living accommodation abroad, it amazed me. This accommodation was reported to be costing $98,400 per year. The parliamentary secretary to the minister thought that was quite a joke. She wanted to know whether the hon. member thought a representative of Canada should live in a tumbledown shack. 1 say we do not want the admiral to live in a tumbledown shack, but we do not want him to be living extravagantly either.
When I became a school teacher and went into a new district there was a depression on and at that time 1 was on the negotiating committee for the teachers. One of the first things I told the school board was that the negotiating committee should not live above the standard of the people in our region. In other words, we should not have a higher standard of living than that of the boys and girls we were teaching. The school board agreed, and there was no difficulty in reaching an agreement on a fair salary for that time. It was not very much
Summer Recess
in those days. It was $750 a year, but it was a fair salary in the light of all conditions.
This admiral should not be living high and mighty above everybody else. An expenditure of $98,000 does not make sense. There are hundreds of people in this country who are not living in shacks but are living in homes they have worked on and improved. I am thinking of the renters, but these people are not renting at this high price. I was shocked at the minister for condoning this type of thing. That is the most serious part of the whole affair. Our civil servants should not be living high above the average of other Canadians. Certainly we want them to live well. They hold important jobs and are important people. But let us not go completely out of line by paying almost $100,000 a year for living quarters in addition to all the other expenses. In my view that is another example of waste.
There is one other item about which many people may not agree. Nevertheless, it bothered me when I read the report which came out the other day. It indicated that we are spending something like $5,000 a day on entertainment in the House of Commons on booze. 1 think that is going very far. 1 realize a drink might be nice for those who want to have a drink at social events, but $5,000 a day on the average, or $2 million a year on booze, is going too far.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I think we should get some accountability and respectability to the people. Thousands of Canadians like a drink and do not mind their members of Parliament having a drink, but they object very seriously to this kind of public money being spent on something that is completely unnecessary. That is the sad story of waste which I wanted to bring to the attention of this House.
When the parliamentary secretary supported the extravagance, she said that they realized neither a shack nor a lean-to were suitable accommodation for a man who represents the finest forces in the world. Neither the hon. member for Leeds-Grenville, nor anyone in this House was suggesting that this admiral should have a lean-to or a shack. We want him to live in good accommodation but not at $100,000 a year at the taxpayers' expense.
The next point I would like to raise is the matter of the two languages. We live in a country founded by two peoples, and the language to each is important. I do not find people in western Canada anti-French, anti-Polish, or anti-Hungarian. Our people come from almost every country of the world. I have a cosmopolitan population in my riding. What people object to are the inequalities which come out of these two languages.
I commend the government for what has happened in Alberta with regard to the two languages. Out of the 17 senior executive positions in Alberta, not one is required to be bilingual. That is proper because it is not necessary. We have a comparatively large number of people who speak French, fine people, but they also speak English. There is no need for both languages in that province. Of all the Canadians I know of French origin, 1 do not know one who does not handle English as well as I do, and many of them far better. Therefore there is no need to have the positions in Alberta calling for bilingual

July 22, 1980
Summer Recess
qualifications. That means that everyone in Alberta, of whatever origin or language, can apply for these positions.
Where the inequality comes is that many senior positions in the federal government are designated as bilingual. That is where many English-speaking people feel they are being discriminated against. They feel there is no opportunity for them to ever get to those positions. I know that some positions must be bilingual, and I agree with that. However, I suggest to the government that if we are going to be equal on both sides, it should review the bilingual positions in the federal government in the capital area with a view to seeing whether it is essential that each of those be filled by someone who speaks and reads French as well as English. If that is the case, it immediately disqualifies hundreds of good Canadians who speak English well, but not French. If it is essential, I do not think they can carry the judgment of our people anywhere. If it is not completely essential, we build up an inequality that helps to build up this wall between the peoples of the two languages.
One other item 1 wish to discuss is the teaching of language by the Public Service Commission. I have the 1977-78 figures. At that time $40 million was spent on language training, $6 million in the armed forces and $9.8 million, totalling $56 million spent on language training. There were 18,426 people who took lessons in the other language. Twenty per cent of these were English taking lessons in French and 80 per cent were Canadians of French or other origin taking lessons in English; 3,600 and 14,700, 18,000 altogether. I do not know how many of those people completed the course to the point where they could handle the language.
In teaching school I found that if I did not stop every once in a while and review what was going on, 1 did not know whether I was being successful or not. I suggest that the Commissioner of Languages is an excellent commissioner, a very fair-minded man who is doing a good job for the administration. If the government would give him authority to review this whole matter we could eliminate these small sections of dissatisfaction and inequalities that may be bothering some Canadians of French, English or some other origin.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are giving me the sign that my time is up. Two minutes? Fine. I want to deal with one other item, that of freight. This is of very deep concern throughout western Canada. In Alberta we pay the apex of freight rates, right at the very top. Manitoba and Saskatchewan are not quite as bad, but almost.
The other day a farmer said to me, "When I ship wool east I pay freight on that; when I buy back the finished product, I also pay the freight." At the western economic conference, and I wish I had another half hour to go into that, the Prime Minister promised that something would be done about freight rates. So far nothing has been done. I ask the government and the Minister of Transport to give the matter of freight rates top priority if they want to build up some credibility in western Canada.

The main issue is that the Liberal party is gambling with the future of this country in going ahead with this pre-build. July 22, 1980
Northern Gas Pipeline

The hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans), in an eloquent speech last night, showed just how important this is to us as the basis of our future prosperity. This is a high stakes poker game, as my hon. friend from Regina will appreciate. I said the government was gambling with our energy security. They are proposing to export Canadian gas to the United States-not to transport 3.2 trillion feet of Alaskan gas but to export Canadian gas. We say it should have been kept here for use in this country. It is said that we in the NDP are not positive, that all we do is criticize. No. We say it could be banked. Today my hon. friend from Yorkton-Melville asked a question in French. He asked whether the minister had considered Quebec and Ontario and the federal government getting together and saying, "Instead of shipping that gas out we will bank it in Alberta and save it for Canadian consumers." During the debate last night two backbenchers heckled and criticized us. I found it absolutely incredible, since both of them were from ridings in Quebec that have over 15 per cent unemployment and are not connected up to Canadian natural gas. Because of this decision I predict they will probably never get Canadian gas and will have to rely on expensive power. It is incredible the Liberal party cannot see through that.
Instead of exporting gas to the United States, instead of selling it out, we could have extended the pipeline to the maritimes. I know there are maritimers in the jury I spoke about out in the country. I think they want Canadian gas in the maritimes so that they can get off expensive oil. It makes
sense to them, but it may not make sense to the government. The people in my part of the country and in the other parts of the country from where my colleagues come, such as Vancouver Island, rely on expensive imported oil. They would like to have Canadian gas as well. They will not get it soon, if the government does not build a pipeline. The government goes north-south instead of east-west. In our view that is a bad mistake.
It is clear that the government is relying on the energy figures of the National Energy Board. Can we really rely on the figures of the National Energy Board, considering that they are supplied by the oil and gas companies, most of which are not Canadian companies but multinational ones? In September, 1970, the Canadian government, on the advice of the National Energy Board, approved the largest natural gas deal in this country's history. Canada agreed to sell 6.3 trillion cubic feet of gas to the United States, and it got $2 billion over the course of the contract. Today that gas is worth $25.2 billion, so Canada lost approximately $23 billion for that sell-out.
As a matter of fact, the oil and gas companies told the Canadian government in 1973 that we had enough oil to last 80 years and enough natural gas to last over 100 years. Acting on this information, the government allowed the sale of three billion barrels of oil between 1974 and 1978, and another three trillion cubic feet of natural gas. Less than a year later the industry returned to the Board and claimed that in eight years Canada would not be able to meet its own needs and therefore the industry needed massive tax cuts to find more oil. So, they told the Board one thing, then came back and told them something else. At the risk of sounding repetitive, let me say that a country must be rather silly to make a mistake once, but it must be crazy to make the same mistake a second time.
The hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) asked the minister various questions. He asked, "Why not gas swaps? If we are to sell this gas now, then require them to give equal amounts later on." The minister said that it was technically impossible. The minister has not stood up and told us why we cannot have gas swaps. In fact no front bench Liberal, no cabinet minister, none of the big boys or the heavy guns, have stood up and told us why we cannot have gas swaps. They have not even taken part in this debate. That is what they think of Parliament and the Canadian public.
We asked for assurances from the United States. When the minister was in opposition he asked for ironclad commitments and assurances. There has been a little debate in the country in the last week about those assurances. I want to say what 1 think Canadians think about these assurances. They do not think they are worth the paper on which they are written. One can even be objective in that and say that one congress does not bind another congress, that President Carter does not bind the future president. The point is that it is not binding at all; there is no deal there at all.
We in this party tried to raise in the context of the debate last week and this week that there is a pattern of assurances in our dealings with the United States. Some of my colleagues
July 22, 1980

have raised this matter. The United States is our great neighbour and friend, but in the last few years there has been a pattern. The question is: can we really take these assurances as being there? We can look at what happened to the assurances respecting fisheries, the auto pact, acid rain and the action on acid rain. The point is that we are not getting anywhere. We had a trump card, we had an ace in our poker hand. What did we do? We went down there and threw it away by allowing the pre-build. We could have postponed the pre-build for at least one year, said that we wanted swaps and adequate assurances, and then we could have dealt with the new administration, whichever it is, in the new Congress. 1 submit we could have had that, but the government gambled that the whole line would be built. I do not think it is a gamble worth taking. It is a reckless gamble.
The government gambled with Parliament. Section 20(4) is not very complicated. Perhaps 1 sound like the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) or some Philadelphia lawyer in saying this, but really that section is quite simple. Parliament authorized the Northern Pipeline Act. It talked about a pipeline bringing gas from Alaska to the lower forty-eight. The government did not come back to Parliament, but it brought in an order in council which did not require a vote or any debate; it just made an announcement. We were the ones who forced the debate. The government was not going to have a debate. By order in council, rubber stamped by the National Energy Board, the government brought in a complete change. It talked about a smaller pipeline exporting Canadian gas to American markets. Last year or the year before, the present Minister of Finance said in the House of Commons that they would consult the House in every part of this act. Numerous ministers, including the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard), before the Standing Committee on Northern Pipelines, said that it was the total pipeline, the whole pipeline.
One could cite chapter and verse, not to mention the fact that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Guigan), when he was writing committee reports for the government, said that they should not bring in legislation like this, that they should not do things like this, and that it was wrong for Parliament. I am a new and young member of Parliament, as are many of my colleagues, and do not have a great deal of parliamentary experience.
Except for the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and a few other members, I do not really see any great concern in the House any more for the rights of Parliament. Maybe that is something in the past about which no one really cares. I care about it because Parliament is the last bastion of freedom. This is it, this is democracy, this is the bottom line. If we go around this, there is nowhere else to go. I see a member putting his head down. I do not think it is funny. 1 think it is important and I think the jury out there in the country thinks it is important too. 1 would bet on that.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 listened with interest to the introduction of the motion by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). I know his area well because 1 am from Vancouver, as the hon. member is, and I am pleased to say that there was at least one sentence in his introduction with which 1 could agree, and that was the commitment of his party-as indeed of the government-to energy self-sufficiency. 1 think perhaps the hon. member had in mind oil self-sufficiency, since we have already achieved energy self-sufficiency in a broad sense, but we are committed to achieving oil self-sufficiency as well.
In other respects, I had difficulty following the statement of the hon. member in introducing his motion. He seemed to be eager to include in his remarks every possible allegation and distortion about the government's energy policy, and in particular about the reasons for the decision to proceed with the pre-build of the pipeline. I fear that it would take me more than the 20 minutes available to respond to his curious potpourri of allegations and distortions. However, let me, for a moment at least, say a word about one or two.
The hon. member alleged that the government is gambling with our sovereignty. He did not in any way substantiate that statement. In one sentence he said that the government is gambling with Canada's sovereignty. What does he mean? He made a statement and left it. There is no evidence whatever in the decision to proceed with the pre-build of the pipeline of any gambling with sovereignty or any sell-out. There is no evidence of that, and the hon. member could not substantiate his statement.
Speaking of allegedly devious acts by the government, he referred to a "sneak-in" of the Syncrude levy. If the hon. member had taken the time to look at the legislation governing the Syncrude levy, he would have seen that there is a formula which is followed and which relates the price paid to the Syncrude producers to world price levels. The other night when the minister introduced his ways and means motion in that regard, the government was simply continuing a practice which the House had accepted and which has been in place for several years.
The hon. member spoke of the need for more use of natural gas in Canada. That is a program which the government has been active in pursuing. The program includes the construction of a natural gas pipeline from Montreal to Quebec City which the minister recently announced. There is also a very real interest on the part of the government in overcoming the environmental problems which have, 1 trust, only temporarily delayed the construction of the pipeline into the maritimes.
The hon. member opposite noted his misgivings about National Energy Board estimates. I find that to be a curious statement on his part because, when NEB estimates substantiate his point of view, he is only too ready to use them. However, on this occasion we find that they are supposedly unsubstantiated and unreliable.
Finally, in his introduction the hon. member opposite referred to a series of letters or telegrams which the government and opposition parties have received on the subject of the pre-build, a question to which I would like to return in a few minutes. However, I do find it odd that we are not supposed to accept the Premier of Alberta as a "real person", that we are not to accept the views of the industry and of trade unions, that we are not to accept the views of university people or any range of Canadians as being in support of this decision, but rather that we are only to accept those who the hon. member says have been in contact with him.
The fact is that the government has decided to proceed with the southern section of the whole Alaska highway natural gas pipeline. The decision was taken to make the whole integrated pipeline possible, and it was taken to spread the construction costs and the demands which the construction will make on the
July 22, 1980

skilled manpower and other resources of this country over a longer period, a period when there will not be so much competition with other massive energy projects which lie immediately ahead for Canada.
Hon. members noted of course that yesterday the National Energy Board, subsequent to the government's decision, decided that the Foothills company has met the financing requirements under the Northern Pipeline Act. The decision to move ahead with the pre-build of the pipeline was not an easy decision. We have recognized, particularly the ministers involved most directly in the decision, that there are risks, but weighed against the substantial economic benefits which are inherent in the decision to proceed with the construction of the southern section of the total pipeline, those risks seem to us well worth the taking.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) referred to the decision as a "judgment call". Indeed it is a judgment call in the sense that a wide variety of benefits and factors had to be weighed. But to govern is to decide, and the government has decided. I, therefore, find it particularly odd that the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway would accuse the government of being all talk and no action. The fact is that the present government has taken action and made its decision, but apparently not to the liking of the hon. member opposite.
I think, through the discussions of the past week, that the benefits to Canadians of the pre-build of the southern portion of the pipeline have become evident. It is known, for example, that Canada will benefit through the construction of this pipeline section which will cost over $600 million. Perhaps more important, 90 per cent of that expenditure will be made in Canada. Indeed, 100 per cent of the expenditure on the pipe as such will be made here at home. Approximately 2,100 man-years of employment will be provided directly through the construction of the pre-build section. Moreover, it has been estimated that 150,000 man-years will be provided directly and indirectly over the period from 1980 to 1984 from the capital expenditures of $1.6 billion required to pre-build the pipeline and instal the necessary production and gathering equipment to support that section of the pipeline.
As I say, it must be evident by now to all Canadians that the benefits of the decision which the government has made and the subsequent conclusion of the National Energy Board to authorize proceeding with the pipeline will bring benefits to all Canadians. The geographic impact has been estimated. The benefits to British Columbia, for example, will be of the magnitude of $70 million; Alberta, $650 million; Saskatchewan and Manitoba together, $360 million; and Ontario and Quebec another $360 million.

The answer is that the government of that day chose to make a deal with persons whom the late John Diefenbaker called "Texas Buccaneers". In other words, the government of that day chose to lend our money to foreign persons so that they could make huge profits out of building a gas pipeline in our country.
