ever in the history of the Canadian House of Commons the rules of this place were so abused and so misused as they were in 1956. It reminds me of an Old Testament story I used to tell in another profession years ago. When Moses complained about the golden calf, Aaron said to Moses, "It is not our fault, we put in the gold and out came the calf'. Today the Prime Minister said that it was not his fault, that the law as it now reads is there for him to use. The fact of the matter is

that it is his fault. He is the head of the government which agreed to an order in council which this government should not have passed. The government says that the authority is there under subsection 20(4). It is true that subsection 20(4) gives the board, subject to the approval of the governor in council, the power to rescind, amend or add to the terms and conditions set out in schedule 111 which are deemed to be such and such, and so on. Yes there is power to change the terms and conditions set out in schedule 111. In schedule III there is condition 12 which provides that the company shall do certain things respecting the pipeline. The pipeline is defined in clause 2 of the bill as a line for the transmission of natural gas from Alaska across Canada, along the route set out in the accompanying documents.

That is all this legislation provides: it provides for nothing else. But the government, using its order in council power, has amended condition 12 of schedule III. The wording of that amendment is to be found on pages 3133 and 3134 of Hansard for Friday, July 18. I invite all members who take this matter seriously to read that order in council. It says that condition 12, as passed by this Parliament, is rescinded or is wiped out and that another one is put in its place. What does this other one include? It includes a provision for a portion of the pipeline. There is no reference in the act to the pipeline being in portions. It is the pipeline, the whole line.

Pipelines are like railroads in that they link the country together. This most recent pipeline, known as the pre-build, is just the first phase of a line which will reach into the far northwest corner of our country when completed. This line will serve a dual duty in that it will not only transport Canadian gas from the far north but will also accommodate the United States in sending their natural resource to the lower 48. The spinoff from this project will be of tremendous benefit to the financial structure of Canada in terms of jobs and cash flow. I am sure time will vindicate the go-ahead on this pipeline. Who would suggest that the first pipeline from the west to the east was anything but a roaring success for Canada?
However, at this point there is simply no way we can develop alternative energy resources fast enough. Canadians will be dependent on oil energy for many years to come.
What about the energy potential in Canada? We have the oil fields in the west and the north, Hibernia off the east coast, and uranium mines, but where do we go from here? Do we harness the power of the ocean tides or recycle garbage? Gasohol and the development of energy resources is paramount to our survival. I am sure that if we have the capability of sending a man to the moon and taking pictures far out in space, we can find other sources of fuel to fire our machines. I look forward to the proposed alternative energy corporation supplying some of those sound choices in the years to come.

We know the salary scales in government agencies and banks. For instance, the salary of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is less than that of the Chief Justice or that of the Auditor General. of Canada and the president of the Federal Business Development Bank, whose salaries are tied into that of the Prime Minister. That result is in the middle-range salary levels where there is a total bleedout of trained personnel.

Where does this all lead? As I have a notice of motion on the order paper, I would advocate to hon. members that we follow the example of our friends in Australia. In 1973 they set up a remuneration review tribunal under the remuneration tribunals act, 1973. This body was named by the governor in council and headed by a state-appointed judge, not a federally appointed one. This tribunal reviews all salaries of judges, Crown corporations and public servants. Also they have a different tribunal which touches on what they call tertiary educational institutions.
I should like to refer to their report of 1979 which reads in part as follows:
We have followed the practice established by the tribunal in past reviews. Advertisements were placed in 16 newspapers indicating the coverage of the review and inviting interested persons, organizations and associations to submit in writing any reviews they consider should be taken into account in the review . . . Also, as in earlier reviews, letters were written to the Prime Minister (inviting an over-all submission from the government)-
The government does not make a decision in this regard. The government is merely a party making a submission to a tribunal. It continues:
-to the leaders of each parliamentary party (inviting a submission from each party), to each member of Parliament (including supplementary requests to each minister inviting submissions on holders of first division offices and holders of public offices within his portfolio), to the Attorney General (inviting a submission relating to judges), to the Chief Justice and to the chief judges of other federal courts, to all first division officers of the public service, and to individual statutory office holders or chairmen of statutory authorities covered by the act.
In 1979 they received 388 written submissions, which was an excellent review and testing of public opinion. Nothing was done on the quiet. They brought in a report. The government made certain comments with regard to the holding of salaries in certain branches, and the commissioner said:
We are not persuaded that we should follow this course.
Then, according to the act, the report is given to a minister who reports on behalf of the tribunal, and within 15 days of its receipt he must table it in the House. The report will take effect, unless within 15 days of its receipt or tabling there shall be passed a motion in either House objecting to it. If the motion objecting carries, it all stops. But the government itself is not party to the appointing of the commission, and it defers its own discretion to some time in the future. The beauty of this is that a professionally constituted and practised body examines the requirements of office and the salaries that should be paid. It is able to weigh them all, one against the other, and maintain a semblance of justice and continuity.

Mr. Speaker, I have to say, as a new member, that 1 am disappointed and, in fact, alarmed at the filibustering nature of the New Democratic Party. I had assumed that these members, both individually and collectively, were interested in the orderly treatment of events. However, even though I know that some members of the New Democratic Party, especially new members, wish to contribute as much as they can, I believe that as a party they act neither for their constituents, their regions, nor for their country. This filibuster by the NDP, which has turned into a pipeline debate, is nothing more than an attempt by the New Democratic Party to attract and keep the attention of the media. If they could not retain the attention of the media in Canada I am sure they would be the first out of the doors. And when I say that they would be first out of the doors, I mean that they, too, as well as the rest of us, have commitments to their constituents.
All too often we all have the tendency to think that the world begins and ends here. But that is not so. As members of Parliament we have an equal commitment to our constituents, and we must never forget it. The NDP is only interested in grandstanding. It is only interested in waving flags of alarm. It is the party which opposes everything. It is the party which has sold its soul to the multinational unions. It is the party which, in 1979, received approximately $150,000 from one international union, and approximately $325,000 from another international union. It is the party which encourages strikes. It is the party whose leader stands in the strike line and says, "Do not go back to work-at least not until the press come".
This is the party which wants to see more unemployment in Ontario. It is the party which wants to see more unemployment in Hamilton. And it is the party which wants to bring industry to its knees. It is the party which wants to bring the Alaska gas pipeline to a halt, the party which believes we should not go ahead with the pipeline unless we can guarantee all the funds before we lift a shovel, guarantee all gas contracts, present and future, before we do any work, and guarantee that all gas prices, present and future, will never change. This is the party which does not believe in the future of Canada and that is why the Canadian people, year after year, election after election, reject them.
Let me state a few facts related to the Alaska highway natural gas pipeline. Exports of natural gas from Canada are not approved by the National Energy Board until they have been certified as surplus to Canada's needs. Our gas exports to the United States are in no way a cut price sale. They are distinctly more expensive than domestic U.S. supplies. We are selling this gas at the highest price possible. Holding up the decision on the southern part of the total project, might just hold up the whole thing since the cash flow generated by the exports from Canada will help finance the northern part. More serious, though, is the attitude the Americans will take to indecision, an indecision which might force them to go elsewhere for their energy source. During 1980, 15 per cent of the total exploration budget for Canadian oil and gas will be invested in the United States. This amounts to $600 million and most of this money will be from small oil companies
Northern Gas Pipeline
departing to the United States. The U.S. gas reserves in Prudhoe Bay represent more than 10 per cent of our established reserves. Surely we recognize the importance of these reserves to the United States.
In Canada direct capital expenditure for the pre-build will be $1.6 billion. Of this, $655 million will go to the pre-build line, and another $935 million to the installation of production mills and other facilities. The pipeline will create employment opportunities between 1980 and 1984 of 150,000 man-years, of which 25 per cent will accrue to Ontario and Quebec, 25 per cent to Manitoba and Saskatchewan, and the remainder to Alberta and B.C. Mr. Speaker, the boost to Canada's balance of payments will be approximately $2 billion a year. Surely we understand that this will help keep interest rates down.
Natural gas reserves in Canada at the present time amount to approximately 70 trillion cubic feet, and this does not include the 10 trillion cubic feet in the Arctic, the five trillion cubic feet in the Mackenzie Delta, and the three trillion cubic feet off the east coast. It is estimated that approximately 50 per cent of all gas wells drilled in Alberta are not tested or proven up, so they are not included in the National Energy Board's reserves. The pre-build pipeline will increase gas production in Alberta by 16 per cent or 18 per cent and the gas companies say they can easily increase it by 50 per cent.
The Alberta Energy Conservation Board now estimates that reserves of gas in Canada could be as high as 160 trillion cubic feet and could even go to 200 trillion cubic feet in the next few years. Mr. Speaker, if momentum is stopped on this pipeline with respect to exploration, development and sale of surplus natural gas, the industry will start to gear down. This will have an effect on the flow of capital, less reserves will be found, unemployment will increase in some areas, technological advances related to new methods for extraction and finding new reserves may slow and, strangely enough, this could be the way to prove the NDP are correct.
I am happy that the government is following up on yet another policy introduced by the previous Conservative government. As proof of this I would like to refer to the statement made by the Hon. Robert de Cotret who, as the minister responsible for the Northern Pipeline Agency, spoke on December 13 last. He mentioned two main points: one, that the government was committed to this pipeline, and, second, that the pre-build was an important component in the completion of the whole line.
For some time now many Albertan members of Parliament have verbally and in written form pressed the government for a decision on the Alaska highway gas pipeline. Of course we are disappointed that it has taken so long to recognize the tremendous benefits to Canada. We are vitally interested in this project. I was more than a little shocked to read in a Calgary paper on July 19 that Senator Olson stated some Albertan members of Parliament were not in favour of this pipeline. I want that Liberal retread to know that no Albertan member of Parliament has opposed the pipeline. They have spoken out for

more action and better information on the details related to the proposed pipeline. It seems that the Senator from Medicine Hat is all wet once again. In conclusion, the Alaska highway natural gas pipeline is a pipeline which will benefit all of Canada and will make the completion of other pipelines in the north and the east, to Ontario and the maritimes, not only a possibility but a probability.

Hon. members opposite shout, "Watch out for your ridings". Let me say that there is no issue on which all
July 22, 1980

members of our party feel more one, comfortable and truly at home-and I think with a majority of Canadians-than on this issue at this particular time in our history.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) speaks of guarantees. Let us look at the statements. Hon. members can read along, if they want to turn their editions of Hansard for July 18 to page 3128. They can read for themselves and Canadians can see for themselves the statement of intention of the producers at Prudhoe Bay. They can see exactly what the position is. They can see the conditions and the statement of intent of these producers. Hon. members should listen to the tremendous commitment that Sohio and Exxon are making to build the Alaska pipeline. Hon. members should listen to the extent of this tremendous commitment:
The producers have indicated willingness to participate in a substantial way with Alaskan northwest in the financing of the Alaskan pipeline and conditioning plan upon reasonable terms and conditions-
God knows what that means.
-provided they are not placed in the position of becoming, in effect, the ultimate guarantors of completion of the ANGTS and provided that their financial exposure is effectively limited.
That is some commitment: "Okay, we will go along with this plan provided we do not have to guarantee it, provided we are not exposed too much, and provided, and provided, and provided". These are the ironclad commitments the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) put down on Thursday night.
Listen to what they go on and say.
If the parties, or any of them, conclude that alternative approaches in financing, or waivers of law under the Alaskan Natural Gas Transportation Act are necessary to effectuate a feasible and effective plan of financing-
Which means they do not now have a feasible and effective plan of financing because, if they had one now, they would not be talking about what they will have in the future.
-such party or parties may develop alternatives and advise appropriate authorities of their conclusions.
That is not exactly what I would call a full-fledged commitment or guarantee. It is so hedged and couched in the terms of what may happen and provisos as to what might happen that it is not even funny, and there is a simple reason for that. There was a previous pipeline in Alaska. There was an oil pipeline in Alaska. Many members of this House from both sides have been to see that pipeline. That pipeline was supposed to cost $1.7 billion. It came in at over $11 billion, and the hard fact of the matter is that as long as Canada is providing the United States with reasonably secure and reasonably cheap supplies of gas, they will have no incentive to go to Alaska. Why should they when they can suck it off us at cost?
The hon. member for Nepean-Carleton, the Wizard of Ooze, came before this House and said, "You have to build a pipeline in stages". There is no argument about that, but what are the stages which are called for in the act? What is in the act which was brought before this Parliament? What is in the agreement which was signed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and James Schlesinger? It is right here in schedule I which refers to expeditious construction and a
Northern Gas Pipeline
timetable: Alaska, January 1, 1980; Yukon main line pipe laying, January 1, 1981. Other construction in Canada is to provide for timely completion of the pipeline to enable initial operation by January 1, 1983. Those are the stages of the line. It is to start in the north at Prudhoe Bay and go all the way south, and because it is starting in stages, one gets down to knowing that that in fact is what the Americans intend to do. They have reneged on that deal.
The Americans have failed to live up to their commitment to build the Alaska pipeline. And what is our punishment? The Prime Minister negotiates and says we are going to get the toughest deal we can on fisheries, on acid rain and on the auto pact, but what is the punishment we are going to mete out to the Americans? We are going to build our stage of the pipeline first so that we can finance the whole damned thing and sell out our natural gas in the course of doing so.
The final argument we get from the Liberal party is with regard to jobs. There is no member of Parliament in this House who is not concerned about jobs. The question is what is the best way to create permanent jobs, and not jobs which disappear as soon as the pipeline is built and not jobs which have no meaning because they are simply short-term jobs.
We are talking about jobs which are based on an industrial strategy because those jobs are renewable, and those jobs make sense because they are not part of some quick fix or reliance on a short-term construction project. When in doubt, build a pipeline: That is the policy of the Liberal party.

The result of the pipeline envy which Fixates hon. members opposite will simply be that the Canadian dollar will go up and up, and our manufacturing competitiveness and our manufacturing industry will be less and less competitive. That is the final bottom line implication of the policy which is being followed.
It was a former Liberal cabinet minister, in the days when there were Liberal cabinet ministers who were not afraid to speak their minds from time to time, Eric Kierans, who wrote an article entitled "The day the Cabinet was misled" published in the March, 1974 "Canadian Forum". I commend to hon. members who want to understand how the cabinet and how this government have been misled and led by their noses by the multinational oil and gas companies for the last 15 years. Mr. Kierans said:
We do object to heavy investments in projects which have the sole objective of selling and exporting our badly needed resources. It would be much wiser to invest our scarce capital in other projects and to negotiate a right-of-way for the Americans to build their own pipeline. That would protect our environment, safeguard native rights and would provide a percentage of the line's capacity to transport Mackenzie Delta gas to Canadian homes and factories.
There is a real difference between investment in a vast construction project which will have a highly distorted effect

Northern Gas Pipeline
on the economy and a program of industrial investment over the whole range of the economy which would provide the industrial structure and the industrial strategy we need.
Under this Liberal government we have a $17 billion deficit in finished goods. We have a government which has consistently increased the portion of our resources that is exported and the portion of our resources which makes up our total exports. The Prime Minister, who is sitting in his chair tonight, has presided over the systematic dismantling of the Canadian economy and its takeover by foreign multinational companies. Who are these multinational companies? Is it any surprise that Shell, Amoco and all those other American companies are buying up our gas and then going to the NEB and saying they would like to take our gas-which is really our gas because we own it-and export it back to their home country? Should that come as any surprise? The hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan), in a speech which was certainly interesting and vital if nothing else, said that the gas industry in Canada was Canadian-owned. That is a false statement because 70 per cent of the gas industry in Canada is owned by foreigners, the vast majority of them Americans.
The reason we are voting on this tonight is very simple. We are insisting on a vote and refusing to leave this House before we have a vote because we want to make it perfectly clear that the New Democratic Party is concerned about the future of our resources and the changing of our economy, and those other twin parties of reaction are concerned only about quick fix and short-term gain.
